opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting one, because Slack is where a lot of the actual work conversation happens. It's not a blank chat window where you start from zero; there's already rich context: threads, channels, who said what, decisions that got made three weeks ago. So the potential is that Claude can be a participant in a team's workflow rather than a tool you go off and consult separately. You can tag it in a thread and say "summarize where we landed on this," or "draft a response to this customer issue," and it has the surrounding conversation to work with. That's a very different interaction pattern from one-on-one chat.

What excites me most is the collaborative aspect. Most of how we've designed these models so far assumes a single user talking to a single assistant. In Slack, you suddenly have multiple people, different goals, sometimes conflicting instructions, all in the same space. That forces you to think about the model's behavior differently. How does it know whose request to prioritize? How does it stay helpful without being noisy? When should it jump in versus stay quiet? Those are really fun product and model-behavior questions.

On the limitations side, a few things come to mind. One is context: Slack workspaces are huge and messy, and the model doesn't automatically see everything, nor should it. There are real permission and privacy questions about which channels and messages it can read, and you want those boundaries respected very strictly. Another is the format itself. Slack is short-form and fast, so long, essay-style answers feel out of place. You have to tune the model to be concise and conversational in a way that fits the medium.

There's also a trust and reliability piece. When Claude says something in a shared channel, it's visible to the whole team, so mistakes or hallucinations carry more weight than in a private chat. You want it to be calibrated: clear about what it knows, what it's inferring, and when someone should double-check.

Longer term, I think the interesting direction is moving from Claude answering questions in Slack to Claude actually doing work: kicking off tasks, following up, connecting to other tools, and reporting back in the thread. That's where it starts to feel less like a chatbot and more like a teammate. But getting there means solving those trust, permission, and social-norm questions well, not just the capability ones.

r001.rationale: It discusses Slack context and summaries, but does not propose tailoring summaries to an individual user’s interests.

r002.rationale: It says Slack’s short-form format calls for concise answers, but does not identify the interface as a constraint on which features Anthropic could build.

r003.rationale: It raises permission, trust, and social-norm concerns, but does not cite avoiding dependence on Slack as a reason Anthropic did not invest further in the integration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so Slack is interesting because it's one of the few places where the model is already sitting inside the context of how people actually work, rather than in a separate tab you have to go to. When I was working on this at Anthropic, the thing that struck me is that most of the interesting signal in a company lives in conversations, not in documents. The doc is the artifact, but the reasoning, the disagreements, the "wait, why did we decide that" — that's all in threads. So if Claude can read a channel and actually follow what's happening, it can do things that feel almost unfair, like summarizing a three-day thread you missed, or pulling out the decision that got buried under forty messages of back and forth.

The potential, I think, is really in that ambient layer. You don't have to formulate a question from scratch. You can just tag it in a thread and say "what did we land on here," and the context is already there. That lowers the activation energy a lot, and I think that's actually the biggest unlock — not that the model is smarter in Slack, but that people use it more because it's where they already are.

The limitations are kind of the flip side of that. Slack is messy. It's full of partial context, inside jokes, people talking past each other, half-finished thoughts. A human reading a channel brings a ton of implicit knowledge about who these people are and what the project is. The model doesn't have that by default, so it can confidently summarize a thread and completely miss that the real decision happened in a DM or a meeting nobody wrote down. There's also a trust question. If the model says something in a public channel, it carries a different weight than if it says it to you privately. A wrong answer in a one-on-one chat is annoying. A wrong answer in a channel with thirty people is a thing you now have to go correct.

And then there's the UX constraint, which honestly I think about a lot. Slack is built around short messages. Claude's natural failure mode is being too long. So you have to be really deliberate about getting it to be concise, to not dump five paragraphs when someone asked a yes-or-no question. A lot of the product work is actually about restraint — knowing when not to respond, when to ask a clarifying question instead of guessing, when to say "I don't have enough context in this channel to answer that."

So I'd say the ceiling is high, because the context is rich and the distribution is already there. But getting it to feel like a good colleague instead of an eager intern who read everything and understood half of it — that's the hard part.

r001.rationale: It describes summarizing threads and finding decisions, but does not say summaries are tailored to an individual user’s interests.

r002.rationale: It identifies Slack’s short-message format as a UX constraint and says Claude must be concise and restrained.

r003.rationale: It gives no reason Anthropic did not invest further in the integration and does not mention avoiding dependence on Slack.

astra-6.text:
I think Slack is an interesting environment because so much of the context for your work already lives there. You could imagine asking Claude to catch you up on a discussion, explain why a decision was made, or help turn a conversation into something actionable. You don’t have to copy everything into a separate chat and explain it again.

But being in Slack doesn’t automatically mean it understands your organization. A conversation might be incomplete, a decision might have changed, or the most important context might never have been written down. So there’s a real difference between summarizing what people said and knowing what the team should do next.

And then there’s the question of when it should participate. If it responds to everything, it becomes noise. I think the useful version is something you can bring into a conversation when you need it, that can show you where its answer came from and ask for clarification when the context isn’t sufficient. Taking actions on behalf of the team requires a much higher level of trust.

r001.rationale: It mentions catching a user up on a discussion, but does not propose tailoring summaries to that individual’s interests.

r002.rationale: It discusses Slack’s context and when Claude should participate, but does not identify Slack’s interface as a constraint on Anthropic’s features.

r003.rationale: It says nothing about avoiding dependence on Slack as a reason Anthropic did not invest further in the integration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Slack is interesting because it’s where a lot of work already happens. You could ask Claude to catch you up on a discussion, pull together the decisions people made, or help turn a messy thread into a concrete next step. You don’t have to move everything into a separate interface.

But having access to a conversation doesn’t necessarily mean understanding the context. Was that a final decision or just someone thinking out loud? Is the relevant information in another channel, or did the team discuss it offline? Those distinctions matter.

So I’d separate helping people understand and draft things from taking actions on their behalf. The first is useful even when the model needs some guidance. The second requires much clearer permissions and ways to check its work. The opportunity is there, but being present in Slack is only one piece of being a useful collaborator.

r001.rationale: It suggests catching up on discussions and summarizing decisions, but does not say to tailor summaries to an individual user’s interests.

r002.rationale: It discusses missing context across channels or offline conversations, but does not identify Slack’s interface as a constraint on possible features.

r003.rationale: It does not mention avoiding dependence on Slack as a reason Anthropic did not invest further in the integration.
